```{r, include = F}
# load any other packages and read data here
library(tidyverse)
library(glue)
library(knitr)
# get names
var_names <- read_csv('../data/biomarker-raw.csv', 
                     col_names = F, 
                     n_max = 2, 
                     col_select = -(1:2)) %>%
  t() %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  rename(name = V1, 
         abbreviation = V2) %>%
  na.omit()

biomarker_clean_without_log_transform_outlier_trim <- read_csv('../data/biomarker-raw.csv', 
         skip = 2,
         col_select = -2L,
         col_names = c('group', 
                       'empty',
                       pull(var_names, abbreviation),
                       'ados'),
         na = c('-', '')) %>%
  filter(!is.na(group)) %>%
  select(group, ados, everything())
```

## Abstract

Write a brief one-paragraph abstract that describes the contents of your write-up.

## Dataset

The biomarker data in this study comes from a selected sample of 154 youth males aged 18 months to 8 years. In the sample, 76 were classified as having autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and 78 were classified as typically developing (TD). The average age of the groups was 5.6 years and 5.7 years respectively. Within the ASD group, the 3 ethnicity classifications making up most of the sample are White (33/76), Hispanic/Latino (26/76) and Multiple Ethnicities/Other (9/76). Within the TD group, the 3 biggest ethnicity classifications were White (40/78), African American/Black (14/78) and Multiple Ethnicities/Other (14/78). Within both groups, a majority of subjects did not have any co-morbid conditions. The only co-morbid condition reported that affected a high number of people was seasonal allergies (30/76 in the ASD group and 17/78 in the TD group). All other co-morbid conditions affected no more than 2 people within each group. Lastly, a vast majority of participants did not report taking psychiatric medications. All other psychiatric medications observed were taken by no more than 2 people.

The data was obtained by performing a fasting blood draw in the morning on the healthy subjects. The blood was then processed and analyzed through a Somascan™ assay to get information on the protein levels. The study obtained the levels of 1317 proteins from each of the 154 subjects, of which 192 proteins did not pass the study's quality control. The data was preprocessed by applying a log10 transformation and then normalizing the data with a z-transformation. Furthermore, outliers with z-scores that were greater than 3 or less than -3 were changed to 3 and -3 respectively.

## Summary of published analysis

The paper used 3 different methods to determine a panel of proteins for identifying ASD. The first method utilized a random forest that was trained 1000 times. Proteins were ranked based on their mean decrease in the Gini index, and the top 10 were selected for the random forest model. The second method utilized multiple t-tests. T-tests were conducted to identify the top 10 proteins with the most significant t-test values for identifying ASD. The last method utilized a correlation approach by calculating the correlation coefficient between protein levels and Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS) scores. The 10 proteins with the highest absolute value correlation coefficients were selected.

From the 3 methods, the paper found 5 proteins that were common across all testing methods. A logistic regression model was fit to these 5 proteins as a baseline for testing the predictive accuracy. Additional proteins that were identified from the other models were added one by one to see if they added any predictive power. The process was repeated 1000 times. Confounding factors were also tested by running t-tests and calculating Spearman's rank correlation.

The 5 core proteins that were flagged as significant in all 3 models were MAPK14, IgD, DERM, EPHB2 and suPAR. 4 additional proteins from the models were found to have increased the predictive power and AUC of the logistic regression model: ROR1, GI24, elF-4H, and ARSB. The AUC value for the model with these 9 proteins was 0.860±0.064. The sensitivity was 0.833±0.118 and the specificity was 0.846±0.118.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  A(154 participants) --> B(1317 protein measurements from participants)
  B --> C(Random Forests for top 10 significant proteins) 
  B --> D(T-tests for top 10 significant proteins)
  B --> E(Correlation calculations for top 10 significant proteins)
  C & D & E --> F(Base logistic regression Model with proteins in hard intersection)
  F --> G(Add other significant proteins 1 by 1 to the model if they increase accuracy)
  G --> H[9 proteins identified as the best panel]
```

## Findings

Summarize your findings here. I've included some subheaders in a way that seems natural to me; you can structure this section however you like.

### Impact of preprocessing and outliers

A couple of important choices were made in the data preprocessing. These were: (1) log-transforming the data, and (2) trimming outliers. These transformations were performed because the several of the distributions of protein levels had very large outliers which would have skewed the analysis. We investigated the distribution of protein levels for 5 proteins (PBEF, Carbonic anhydrase III, FGF-8B, TRAIL R1, and CNTN2) and observed a noticeable right skew in all of them. Below is a distribution of 1 of proteins observed.

```{r}
ggplot(data = biomarker_clean_without_log_transform_outlier_trim, aes(x = PBEF)) + 
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 100) + 
  labs(x = "PBEF Level", y = "Frequency", title = "Distribution of PBEF Protein Levels")
```
Because of the skew of the raw protein levels, a log-transform would help transform the data to be more symmetric for the tests completed.

We also investigated the data before trimming outliers. Despite nearly every participant having some number of proteins with outlier levels (>3 standard deviations from the mean), only 8 have more than 80 outliers, while the rest have under 50.

```{r}
proteins_only <- biomarker_clean_without_log_transform_outlier_trim %>% select(-c(group, ados))
means <- colMeans(proteins_only , na.rm = TRUE)
sds   <- sapply(proteins_only , sd, na.rm = TRUE)

outliers_per_subject <- biomarker_clean_without_log_transform_outlier_trim  %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(outliers = sum(abs(c_across(names(proteins_only)) - means) > 3 * sds, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  ungroup()

barplot(outliers_per_subject %>% arrange(outliers %>% desc()) %>% pull(outliers), ylab = "Number of Outliers", xlab = "Participants", main = "Number of Outlier Protein Levels per Participant")
```


Lastly, we looked at the number of outliers in each group. Since the number of outliers did not seem to significantly differ between the ASD and TD groups, trimming outliers should not bias the data in one direction too much.

```{r}
outliers_by_group <- outliers_per_subject %>%
  group_by(group) %>%
  rename(Group = group) %>% 
  summarize("# of Average Outliers" = round(mean(outliers), 2), "Total Outliers" = sum(outliers))
outliers_by_group %>% kable()
```
